claim: In a subagent file only `name` and `description` are required; every other frontmatter field is optional.
why: The reference table marks all other fields No, so a minimal valid subagent inherits all tools, the default model order and the session permission mode.
check: Flag subagents that rely on every default (no `tools`, no `model`) when their purpose is narrow, since valid is not the same as well made.
quote: Only `name` and `description` are required.

claim: Subagent frontmatter is camelCase and an unrecognized or misspelled field is silently ignored with no error.
why: A typo such as `max_turns` or `disallowed-tools` therefore leaves the intended restriction off while the file still loads.
check: Compare each field name in every agent file against the supported list; any near-miss spelling means a restriction is not applied.
quote: Claude Code ignores a field it doesn't recognize without reporting an error.

claim: Besides `name`, `description` and the body prompt, the supported subagent fields are tools, disallowedTools, model, permissionMode, mcpServers, hooks, maxTurns, autoCompactWindow, skills, initialPrompt, memory, effort, background, omitClaudeMd and isolation, plus color and experimental (cacheTtl) in files.
why: This is the complete set the docs list; `color` and `experimental` are accepted in files but ignored in `--agents` JSON.
check: Any field outside this list in an agent file has no effect.
quote: `description`, `tools`, `disallowedTools`, `model`, `permissionMode`, `mcpServers`, `hooks`, `maxTurns`, `autoCompactWindow`, `skills`, `initialPrompt`, `memory`, `effort`, `background`, `omitClaudeMd`, and `isolation`.

claim: If a subagent omits `tools` it inherits every tool available to subagents, including MCP tools.
why: Omission is the permissive default, so a read-only role must state its allowlist or denylist explicitly.
check: Flag reviewer, researcher or explorer subagents with no `tools` or `disallowedTools`, which can edit files and call every MCP tool.
quote: Inherits every tool available to subagents if omitted.

claim: When both `tools` and `disallowedTools` are set, the denylist is applied first, then the allowlist is resolved against what remains, and a tool in both is removed.
why: This order determines the final tool set when the two fields overlap.
check: Look for agents listing a tool in `tools` that is also in `disallowedTools`; the tool is silently unavailable.
quote: If both are set, `disallowedTools` is applied first, then `tools` is resolved against the remaining pool. A tool listed in both is removed.

claim: A `disallowedTools` entry with a specifier such as `Bash(git push *)` removes the whole Bash tool from the subagent, not only the matching commands.
why: To block specific commands while keeping Bash, the docs say to use a Bash deny rule in `permissions.deny`, which applies to the main conversation and subagents.
check: Flag `disallowedTools: Bash(...)` entries that were meant as command-level filters; they disable Bash entirely.
quote: A `disallowedTools` entry with a specifier, such as `Bash(git push *)`, still removes the whole tool from the subagent, not only the matching commands.

claim: A subagent with no `model` runs on the model of the conversation that starts it; when several sources set a model the order is per-invocation `model` parameter, then the definition's `model` (including `inherit`), then `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL`, then the parent's model.
why: The default means a subagent spawned from an expensive main model is itself expensive unless a cheaper model is set.
check: For high-volume or simple roles (search, log reading, formatting), check that `model` is set to a cheaper alias; flag roster-wide omission.
quote: The per-invocation `model` parameter, which Claude can pass when it starts the subagent.

claim: Routing tasks to faster, lower-cost models such as Haiku is a stated reason to define subagents, and a user or project subagent named `Explore` with `model: haiku` overrides the built-in Explore.
why: Cost control by model routing is one of five listed benefits of subagents.
check: Check whether exploration-heavy setups leave Explore on the parent model when a cheaper override would do.
quote: so define one with `model: haiku` to run exploration on a lower-cost model.

claim: The built-in Explore and Plan subagents start without CLAUDE.md files and the git status snapshot; other built-in and custom subagents load both unless `omitClaudeMd` is set.
why: Skipping them keeps research fast and inexpensive.
check: A custom read-only searcher that loads a large CLAUDE.md on every spawn is paying context it may not need; consider `omitClaudeMd: true`.
quote: Explore and Plan start without your CLAUDE.md files and the git status snapshot to keep research fast and inexpensive.

claim: When the combined `description` fields of non-built-in subagents exceed 15,000 tokens, Claude Code warns at startup but still loads every subagent.
why: Descriptions sit in the main context all the time, so the docs say to keep them short and move detail into the body, which loads only when the subagent runs.
check: Sum description lengths across user, project and plugin agents; long descriptions that contain instructions belong in the body.
quote: When the combined descriptions of your subagents, except the built-in ones, exceed 15,000 tokens

claim: A non-fork subagent starts in a fresh context window and does not see the conversation history, invoked skills, or files the main session already read; it works only from the delegation message Claude writes.
why: Isolation is what protects the main context, but it means the delegation prompt must carry everything the worker needs.
check: Check agent bodies and delegation habits for assumptions like 'as discussed' that a fresh worker cannot resolve.
quote: Each subagent starts with a fresh, isolated context window. It doesn't see your conversation history, the skills you've already invoked, or the files Claude has already read.

claim: A non-fork subagent's initial context contains its own system prompt (not the Claude Code system prompt), the task message, the full CLAUDE.md hierarchy (including user, local, managed and AGENTS.md files), a git status snapshot, preloaded skills, and a sibling roster when SendMessage is available.
why: Instruction files therefore reach subagents too, which costs tokens per spawn and also means rules in CLAUDE.md apply to workers.
check: Check whether CLAUDE.md is large enough that every spawned worker pays for it, and whether subagent prompts duplicate rules CLAUDE.md already gives.
quote: including `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, project rules, `CLAUDE.local.md`, managed policy files, and any

claim: A subagent does not inherit the main session's output style or auto memory, and its context window is sized by its own model rather than the parent's.
why: The subagent runs its own system prompt; persistent memory for it must come from the `memory` field.
check: Do not credit a setup for output-style rules reaching subagents; check that long-input subagents are on a model with an adequate window.
quote: **Output style**: a subagent runs its own system prompt, so your

claim: A custom subagent receives only its own system prompt plus basic environment details such as the working directory, not the Claude Code system prompt.
why: The agent body is therefore the whole behavioral specification and must be self-sufficient on tool use, output format and stopping criteria.
check: Read each agent body as if it were the entire prompt; flag bodies that assume default Claude Code behavior.
quote: Subagents receive only this system prompt plus basic environment details like the working directory, not the Claude Code system prompt.

claim: `omitClaudeMd: true` starts a subagent without user, project and local CLAUDE.md (managed policy files still load) and is intended for subagents that take everything from the delegation prompt.
why: It trims context for narrow workers; it is ignored when the agent runs as the main session via `--agent`.
check: Suggest it for self-contained mechanical workers; flag use where the worker needs project conventions that exist only in CLAUDE.md.
quote: Use it for subagents that take everything they need from the delegation prompt.

claim: The `skills` field injects the full content of each listed skill (up to 32 names) into the subagent at startup, but does not restrict which other skills the subagent can invoke through the Skill tool.
why: Preloading gives domain knowledge without discovery; restricting skill access requires omitting `Skill` from `tools` or denying it.
check: Check that preloaded skills are small and relevant to the role; flag long skill lists that bloat every spawn.
quote: The full skill content is injected, not only the description. Subagents can still invoke unlisted project, user, and plugin skills through the Skill tool

claim: Skills that set `disable-model-invocation: true` cannot be preloaded into a subagent through `skills`.
why: Preloading draws from the same set of skills Claude can invoke.
check: Flag a `skills:` list naming a manual-only skill; it will be skipped.
quote: since preloading draws from the same set of skills Claude can invoke.

claim: Plugin-supplied subagents ignore the `hooks`, `mcpServers` and `permissionMode` frontmatter fields.
why: Security: the docs say to copy the file into `.claude/agents/` or `~/.claude/agents/` if those fields are needed.
check: Flag plugin agents relying on those fields for safety restrictions; they are not enforced.
quote: For security reasons, plugin subagents don't support the `hooks`, `mcpServers`, or `permissionMode` frontmatter fields.

claim: A subagent's `permissionMode` is overridden by the main session when it is in bypassPermissions, acceptEdits or auto mode, and a plan-mode parent keeps the subagent in plan mode; unset, the subagent inherits the parent's mode.
why: The parent's mode takes precedence, so a frontmatter `permissionMode` is not a reliable tightening mechanism.
check: Do not accept `permissionMode: plan` or `default` as a safety control when the user normally runs in acceptEdits or auto; use `tools` or hooks.
quote: the subagent runs in that same mode and Claude Code ignores the `permissionMode` you set.

claim: Setting `memory` on a subagent automatically enables Read, Write and Edit and injects the first 200 lines or 25KB of its MEMORY.md; `project` scope is the recommended default.
why: Write access arrives implicitly, which matters for agents meant to be read-only.
check: Flag read-only reviewers that also set `memory`; they gain Write and Edit.
quote: Read, Write, and Edit tools are automatically enabled so the subagent can manage its memory files.

claim: `maxTurns` caps agentic turns; when reached, the output is returned marked partial and Claude can resume the subagent.
why: It bounds runaway workers without discarding their work.
check: Check open-ended exploration or loop-prone agents for a `maxTurns` bound; absence means no cap.
quote: When the subagent reaches the limit, Claude Code returns its output marked as partial, and Claude can

claim: By default a subagent Claude spawns from the main conversation starts in the background, and `background: true` keeps it there even when Claude asks to wait.
why: Results then reach Claude as a completion notification in a later turn rather than blocking the turn.
check: Check designs that need the result before the next step; with fork mode on, Claude cannot wait in interactive sessions.
quote: With nothing configured, a subagent that Claude spawns from your main conversation starts in the background.

claim: Background subagents keep only a reduced built-in tool set (plus all MCP tools), so the same definition can resolve to different tools in foreground and background.
why: Tools outside the list are removed silently, even when named in `tools`.
check: Check agents that list tools such as AskUserQuestion or Workflow and are expected to run in the background; those tools are gone.
quote: Claude Code removes every other built-in tool from a background subagent, whether inherited or listed in the `tools` field, so the same definition can resolve to different tools in the foreground and the background.

claim: Subagents never get AskUserQuestion, EndConversation, EnterPlanMode, ScheduleWakeup, WaitForMcpServers or Workflow, and ExitPlanMode only in plan mode; Agent is withheld at the depth limit.
why: These tools are removed even when listed in `tools`.
check: Flag agent bodies that tell the worker to ask the user questions or launch workflows; the worker cannot.
quote: The first filter removes these tools, even when listed in the `tools` field:

claim: The `Agent(worker, researcher)` spawn allowlist in `tools` works only for an agent running as the main thread via `--agent`; inside a regular subagent definition any type list is ignored.
why: A subagent listing `Agent` can spawn any subagent type while depth allows.
check: Flag subagents using `Agent(x)` to constrain delegation; omit `Agent` entirely to forbid nesting.
quote: The `Agent(agent_type)` allowlist syntax applies only to an agent running as the main thread with `claude --agent`.

claim: Subagents can by default spawn their own subagents up to three layers below the main conversation; `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH=1` turns nesting off.
why: At the limit the subagent does the work itself and returns one summary.
check: Flag cost-sensitive setups with unrestricted nesting; omit `Agent` from read-only or leaf workers.
quote: By default, a subagent can spawn subagents of its own, up to three layers below the main conversation.

claim: Spawning a subagent fails with `Concurrent subagent limit reached` once 20 are running (configurable with `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS`), and there is no cap on the total spawned over a session.
why: The limit applies to running subagents, not cumulative ones.
check: Check fan-out designs that assume more than 20 simultaneous Agent-tool workers; workflows use separate limits.
quote: By default, when 20 subagents are running in a session, spawning another with the Agent tool fails with `Concurrent subagent limit reached`

claim: Use a subagent when a side task would flood the main conversation with output you will not reference again, and define a custom one when you keep spawning the same kind of worker with the same instructions.
why: The subagent absorbs the verbose work and returns only a summary.
check: Judge each agent against this: does it isolate verbose output or enforce constraints, or is it a persona that adds nothing over the main session?
quote: Use one when a side task would flood your main conversation with search results, logs, or file contents you won't reference again: the subagent does that work in its own context and returns only the summary.

claim: Subagents cost tokens twice over: each spends tokens of its own, and every returned report lands in the main context.
why: Many subagents returning detailed results can consume significant main context.
check: Check delegation prompts and agent bodies for a bounded return format (summary, not full dumps).
quote: Running many subagents that each return detailed results can consume significant context, and each subagent spends tokens of its own while it runs.

claim: A fork inherits the entire conversation, system prompt, tools and model of its parent and shares its prompt cache, so it costs less than a fresh subagent for tasks needing the same context; a fork cannot spawn further forks.
why: Identical system prompt and tool definitions let the first request reuse the parent's cache.
check: Where a custom subagent exists only to receive a large pasted context, a fork may be cheaper and simpler.
quote: Because of that reuse, a fork costs less than a fresh subagent for tasks that need the same context.

claim: With `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE=1`, the `model` field in every subagent definition is ignored and Claude cannot pass a model when spawning.
why: The forced model applies to all subagents, teammates and workflow agents.
check: If the force variable is set, per-agent `model` choices in the roster are dead configuration.
quote: Claude Code ignores the `model` field in subagent definitions, and Claude can't pass a model when it starts a subagent.

claim: Subagents inherit the main conversation's extended thinking configuration; there is no per-subagent thinking setting, only the `effort` field.
why: Thinking depth is tuned through `effort`, not a thinking field.
check: Flag agent files that attempt a thinking setting; it does nothing.
quote: There is no per-subagent thinking setting.

claim: A subagent with no `effort` field runs at the session's effort level only when it is on the main conversation's model; on another model that level does not apply.
why: Effort levels depend on the model, so a Haiku subagent does not receive the session's level.
check: For cheap-model workers that need deliberate reasoning, check `effort` is set explicitly.
quote: On the main conversation's model, the subagent runs at the level you pick in the session, such as with `/effort`, or set with `--effort`.

claim: When subagents share a name, the higher-priority location wins in the order managed settings, `--agents`, project `.claude/agents/`, user `~/.claude/agents/`, plugin.
why: A project agent can shadow a user one, and a managed one overrides both.
check: Look for same-named agents across scopes (including nested project directories, where the closest wins) that hide one another.
quote: When multiple subagents share the same name, Claude Code uses the one from the higher-priority location.

claim: Two agent files in the same `.claude/agents/` tree with the same `name` result in only one loading, chosen by filesystem read order.
why: Identity comes from `name`, not the file path or folder.
check: Flag duplicate or near-duplicate names in a roster; behavior is nondeterministic.
quote: Claude Code loads only one of them, chosen by filesystem read order rather than a documented precedence.

claim: A subagent file that has a `name` but no `description` is skipped, with the reason written only to the debug log.
why: A file without `name` is treated as documentation kept beside the agents.
check: Verify every file in agents directories has `name` and `description` and that the opening `---` is the first line.
quote: **A `name` but no `description`**: Claude Code skips the file and writes the reason to the debug log.

claim: Each subagent description should be specific enough to route to exactly one subagent, and each subagent should excel at one task.
why: Claude uses the description to decide when to delegate, so overlapping descriptions cause misrouting.
check: Look for roster members whose descriptions overlap (generic reviewer vs code-reviewer) as redundancy, and for descriptions that never say when to use the agent.
quote: Make each description specific enough to route to the right subagent

claim: Limit each subagent's tool access to only what it needs, for security and focus.
why: The docs list tool limits as a core reason to use subagents and a best practice.
check: Flag write-capable agents whose purpose is analysis, and read-only roles that inherit everything.
quote: **Limit tool access:** grant only necessary permissions for security and focus

claim: To allow some operations of a tool while blocking others in a subagent, use a `PreToolUse` hook that validates the call and exits with code 2, rather than relying on the prompt alone.
why: The docs describe the hook as a backstop to a prompt that already tells the agent to refuse writes.
check: Flag agents whose only protection against writes is a sentence in the prompt.
quote: For more dynamic control over tool usage, use `PreToolUse` hooks to validate operations before they execute.

claim: Frontmatter hooks of a project subagent are skipped, with only a debug-log error, until the folder containing the agent file is trusted.
why: Trust of a parent folder is not enough and a `-p` session does not count as trusted.
check: In CI or `-p` runs, a safety hook defined in project agent frontmatter may not be running.
quote: Until you trust the folder, the subagent still runs, but Claude Code skips its frontmatter hooks and logs an error to the debug log

claim: Define an MCP server inline in a subagent's `mcpServers` rather than in `.mcp.json` to keep its tool descriptions out of the main conversation.
why: The subagent gets the tools and the parent conversation does not pay their context cost.
check: Flag MCP servers used only by one specialist but configured globally, where their tool schemas load every session.
quote: To keep an MCP server out of the main conversation entirely and avoid its tool descriptions consuming context there, define it inline here rather than in `.mcp.json`.

claim: Each subagent invocation creates a new instance; to continue earlier work Claude must resume it, and the built-in Explore and Plan agents are one-shot and cannot be resumed.
why: Resumed subagents keep their full prior history; one-shot agents return no agent ID.
check: For multi-step follow-up work, flag use of Explore or Plan where a custom or general-purpose agent is needed.
quote: The built-in Explore and Plan agents are one-shot and return no agent ID, so Claude can't resume them.

claim: `isolation: worktree` runs the subagent in a temporary git worktree, branched by default from the default branch rather than the parent's HEAD, and the worktree is removed if the subagent makes no changes.
why: It lets parallel workers edit the same repository without overwriting each other.
check: Check parallel write-capable agents for isolation; also note the worktree does not carry the parent's uncommitted state.
quote: The worktree is automatically cleaned up if the subagent makes no changes

claim: With agent teams enabled, a subagent Claude names launches as a teammate, so teams can form without the user asking.
why: Claude may name subagents on its own so it can message them later; teams are experimental.
check: If `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1` is set, expect delegations to turn into costlier teammates.
quote: and while agent teams are enabled, a subagent that Claude names launches as a teammate, so teams can form even when you didn't ask for one.

claim: When a subagent definition is reused as a teammate, its `skills` are not applied, and `mcpServers` apply only to split-pane teammates.
why: Teammates load skills and MCP servers from project and user settings instead.
check: Do not rely on `skills:` preloading for roles also used as teammates.
quote: **`skills`**: Claude Code doesn't apply the definition's `skills` to a teammate in either display mode.

claim: In non-interactive `-p` mode Claude does not spawn teammates, and a subagent Claude names runs as an ordinary subagent even with agent teams enabled.
why: Spawning teammates requires an interactive session.
check: For headless pipelines do not design around teammates.
quote: Claude doesn't spawn teammates, and a subagent that Claude names runs as an ordinary

claim: Use the main conversation rather than a subagent when phases share significant context such as planning, implementation and testing.
why: A non-fork subagent starts fresh and may need time to gather context; iterative work gains nothing from isolation.
check: Flag rosters that split planner, implementer and tester into separate subagents for a single tightly coupled task.
quote: Multiple phases share significant context, such as planning, implementation, and testing

claim: Subagents fit work that is self-contained and can return a summary, produces verbose output, or needs enforced tool restrictions.
why: These are the cases where isolation and restricted tools pay off.
check: An agent whose work needs constant back-and-forth with the user or main context is a poor candidate.
quote: The work is self-contained and can return a summary

claim: Claude Code has five parallel-work mechanisms: subagents, agent view, agent teams, dynamic workflows and projects, differing in who coordinates and whether workers talk to each other.
why: Subagents report to the spawner, agent view sessions report only to the user, teammates message each other, and a workflow script holds the plan.
check: Check that the chosen mechanism matches the work, for example agent teams used where plain subagents would do.
quote: A job outgrows a handful of subagents, or you want findings verified against each other: a codebase-wide audit, a 500-file migration, cross-checked research, or a plan drafted from several angles

claim: Running several sessions or subagents at once multiplies token usage.
why: Each worker has its own context and requests.
check: Weigh any parallel design against the plan's usage limits.
quote: Running several sessions or subagents at once multiplies token usage.

claim: Agent teams do not isolate teammates in worktrees, so work must be partitioned so each teammate owns different files.
why: Two teammates editing the same file leads to overwrites.
check: Check team prompts for explicit file ownership per teammate.
quote: Agent teams don't isolate teammates in worktrees, so

claim: Agent teams are experimental, disabled by default, and have known limitations around session resumption, task coordination and shutdown.
why: They need `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1`.
check: Flag production workflows that depend on teams.
quote: Agent teams are experimental and disabled by default.

claim: Agent teams use significantly more tokens and add coordination overhead; for sequential tasks, same-file edits or many dependencies a single session or subagents work better.
why: Each teammate is a separate Claude instance with its own context.
check: Flag team use on sequential or tightly coupled work.
quote: For sequential tasks, same-file edits, or work with many dependencies, a single session or

claim: Agent teams pay off for research and review, new modules with separate ownership, debugging with competing hypotheses, and cross-layer changes.
why: These tasks let teammates work independently and then challenge each other's findings.
check: Compare the team's task with these four shapes.
quote: Agent teams are most effective for tasks where parallel exploration adds real value.

claim: Start with 3-5 teammates; three focused teammates often outperform five scattered ones, and 5-6 tasks per teammate keeps everyone productive.
why: Token cost scales linearly and coordination overhead rises with team size.
check: Flag teams of many teammates or tasks too small or too large for a clear deliverable.
quote: Start with 3-5 teammates for most workflows.

claim: Teammates load CLAUDE.md, MCP servers and skills like a regular session but do not inherit the lead's conversation history, so spawn prompts must carry task-specific context.
why: A teammate receives only the spawn prompt from the lead.
check: Check spawn prompts for the objective, scope and constraints.
quote: Teammates load project context automatically, including CLAUDE.md, MCP servers, and skills, but they don't inherit the lead's conversation history.

claim: Per-teammate permission modes cannot be set at spawn; teammates start in the lead's mode, including bypassPermissions.
why: A lead run with `--dangerously-skip-permissions` passes that to every teammate.
check: Flag teams launched under bypassPermissions.
quote: You can't set per-teammate permission modes at spawn time.

claim: There are no nested teams and the lead is fixed for the session's lifetime.
why: Only the lead manages the team, and one team exists per session.
check: Do not design hierarchical team structures.
quote: teammates cannot spawn their own teammates. Only the lead can manage the team.

claim: New users of agent teams should start with research or review tasks that have clear boundaries and need no code writing.
why: They show the value of parallel exploration without the coordination problems of parallel implementation.
check: Be wary of teams whose first use is parallel code edits.
quote: start with tasks that have clear boundaries and don't require writing code: reviewing a PR, researching a library, or investigating a bug.

claim: In a dynamic workflow a script, not Claude, holds the loop, branching and intermediate results, so Claude's context holds only the final answer.
why: With subagents, skills and teams Claude is the orchestrator and every result enters a context window.
check: For fan-outs over dozens of items, check whether a workflow would spare the main context.
quote: A workflow script holds the loop, the branching, and the intermediate results itself, so Claude's context holds only the final answer.

claim: Workflows can raise result quality through a repeatable pattern, such as independent agents adversarially reviewing each other's findings or drafting a plan from several angles.
why: This yields a more trustworthy result than a single pass.
check: Prefer a workflow over ad hoc subagents when findings need cross-verification.
quote: it can have independent agents adversarially review each other's findings before they're reported

claim: A workflow run can use meaningfully more tokens than doing the same task in conversation.
why: Many agents are spawned; the docs advise running a small slice first and watching per-agent token use in `/workflows`.
check: Check for unbounded workflow prompts over whole repos.
quote: A workflow spawns many agents, so a single run can use meaningfully more tokens than working through the same task in conversation.

claim: Workflows are capped at 1,000 agents per run, 16 concurrent agents by default and 4,096 items per parallel() or pipeline() call; a Large workflow warning appears past 25 agents or 1.5 million projected tokens.
why: The caps bound runaway scripts; the warning is advisory only.
check: Check fan-out designs against these numbers.
quote: When a workflow schedules more than 25 agents, or its projected token total passes 1.5 million

claim: The workflow size guideline defaults to medium (fewer than 10 agents), or small (fewer than 5) on Pro plans, and is advice to Claude rather than a cap.
why: A prompt calling for a different scale overrides it.
check: Check `workflowSizeGuideline` settings against cost goals.
quote: The default is `medium`, or `small` when you're signed in on a Pro plan with Claude Code v2.1.271 or later.

claim: Turning on `/effort ultracode` makes Claude plan a workflow for every substantive task, raising tokens per request and reaching usage limits sooner.
why: It also suppresses the Large workflow warning and the concurrent subagent limit.
check: Flag ultracode set as a permanent default in `settings.json`.
quote: This applies to every task in the session, so each request uses more tokens and takes longer than the same request without a workflow.

claim: The `ultracode` keyword does not start a workflow from `-p` prompts, scheduled task prompts, or webhook and PR comment payloads.
why: It is an opt-in only for prompts a human types.
check: Headless automation that expects the keyword to fan out will run a normal turn.
quote: It doesn't start a workflow when it reaches the session another way:

claim: Workflow agents choose models in the subagent order, so an unset stage runs on the session model; the docs advise cheaper models for stages that do not need the strongest.
why: A model the script names for a stage counts as the per-invocation model.
check: Check large-run prompts and saved workflows for model assignment per stage.
quote: A model the script names for a stage counts as the per-invocation model in that order.

claim: In headless `-p` runs, workflows start only if the Workflow tool call passes permission evaluation (an allow rule, auto mode, bypass, hook or host approval).
why: No approval prompt is ever shown in `-p` or the Agent SDK.
check: Check CI workflows for a `Workflow` allow rule.
quote: In `claude -p` and the Agent SDK, Claude Code never shows this prompt.

claim: `--bare` is the recommended mode for scripted and SDK calls and skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, subagents, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and CLAUDE.md.
why: It gives the same result on every machine and starts faster.
check: Flag CI scripts using plain `claude -p` that load whatever a host has configured; custom agents need `--agents`.
quote: `--bare` is the recommended mode for scripted and SDK calls, and will become the default for `-p` in a future release.

claim: In bare mode Claude cannot run background commands or background subagents.
why: The limits tied to `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BACKGROUND_TASKS` apply.
check: Do not combine `--bare` with designs that depend on background subagents.
quote: Claude can't run background commands or background subagents

claim: A `claude -p` run waits for background subagents and workflows, but stops after 10 minutes of continuous idle waiting by default and drops the partial result.
why: `CLAUDE_CODE_PRINT_BG_WAIT_CEILING_MS` changes the cap.
check: Long background subagents in scripts need a raised ceiling.
quote: Claude Code stops whatever is still running after 10 minutes of continuous idle waiting by default and drops its partial result.

claim: For unattended runs use `--permission-prompts none` so anything that would prompt is denied and Claude is told not to retry, instead of waiting on a host.
why: Without it a run with a permission host waits for an answer.
check: Check scheduled or CI invocations for a deny-instead-of-prompt configuration.
quote: Pass `--permission-prompts none` when nobody is available to answer permission prompts, for example in a scheduled job.

claim: `/goal` decides completion with a separate evaluator model that judges only what Claude has surfaced in the conversation; it does not run commands or read files.
why: A fresh model checks the condition instead of the one doing the work.
check: Check that goal conditions name a measurable end state and a check whose output appears in the transcript.
quote: It doesn't run commands or read files independently, so write the condition as something Claude's own output can demonstrate.

claim: To bound a goal, put a turn or time clause in the condition; evaluation tokens are billed on the small fast model and are typically negligible.
why: Without a bound the goal runs until met or judged impossible.
check: Flag goals with no stop clause on open-ended work.
quote: To bound how long a goal runs, include a turn or time clause in the condition

claim: If a subagent or background shell command is still running when a turn ends, `/goal` skips evaluation for that turn.
why: Check-ins start after 30 minutes by default.
check: Goals combined with long background subagents may stall between check-ins.
quote: If a subagent or a background shell command is still running when a turn ends, Claude Code skips the evaluation for that turn.

claim: Session-scoped recurring tasks expire 7 days after creation, fire only while Claude Code is running and idle, and one session holds at most 50.
why: This bounds forgotten loops; durable scheduling needs cloud, Desktop or GitHub Actions.
check: Flag `/loop` used for work that must survive closing the terminal.
quote: Recurring tasks automatically expire 7 days after creation.

claim: Use cloud scheduled tasks for work that must run without your machine, Desktop tasks for local files and tools, and `/loop` for quick polling in a session.
why: Only cloud tasks need neither the machine on nor an open session.
check: Match each scheduled job to the right tier.
quote: Use **cloud tasks** for work that should run reliably without your machine.

claim: Monitor, which streams a background script's output, avoids polling and is often more token-efficient than re-running a prompt on an interval.
why: A polling `/loop` pays a full prompt turn per iteration.
check: Flag `/loop` polling for events a Monitor watch could report.
quote: which avoids polling altogether and is often more token-efficient and responsive than re-running a prompt on an interval.

claim: Find the simplest solution and add complexity only when needed; agentic systems trade latency and cost for task performance, and optimizing a single LLM call is often enough.
why: Agents carry higher cost and compounding errors.
check: Flag elaborate multi-agent rosters for tasks one session handles.
quote: When building applications with LLMs, we recommend finding the simplest solution possible, and only increasing complexity when needed.

claim: Orchestrator-workers fits tasks whose subtasks cannot be predicted in advance, while parallelization fits subtasks that can be divided up front or multiple perspectives for confidence.
why: The orchestrator decides subtasks from the input, unlike fixed parallel sectioning.
check: Match the delegation pattern to whether the subtasks are known beforehand.
quote: complex tasks where you can’t predict the subtasks needed

claim: Evaluator-optimizer fits when there are clear evaluation criteria and iterative refinement gives measurable value; the two signs are that a human's feedback demonstrably improves the output and that the model can give such feedback.
why: These are the two signs of good fit.
check: Flag reviewer-fixer loops with no stated criteria.
quote: The two signs of good fit are, first, that LLM responses can be demonstrably improved when a human articulates their feedback; and second, that the LLM can provide such feedback.

claim: Routing easy questions to a smaller model and hard ones to a stronger model is a recommended cost pattern.
why: It optimizes performance per cost; the post names Haiku 4.5 and Sonnet 4.5, and notes its tooling is dated.
check: Check whether cheap and strong roles are separated by model.
quote: Routing easy/common questions to smaller, cost-efficient models like Claude Haiku 4.5 and hard/unusual questions to more capable models like Claude Sonnet 4.5 to optimize for best performance.

claim: The post carries a notice that much of its tooling landscape has changed since December 2024, so its patterns are conceptual and its tool details are dated.
why: Current Claude Code docs supersede it on mechanics.
check: Prefer the Claude Code docs where they differ on mechanics.
quote: Note: Much of the tooling landscape described in this post has changed since December 2024.

claim: Anthropic measured agents using about 4x more tokens than chat and multi-agent systems about 15x more, so multi-agent work needs tasks valuable enough to pay for it.
why: Multi-agent systems work mainly by spending enough tokens; token usage alone explained 80% of BrowseComp variance.
check: Ask whether the task value justifies roughly an order of magnitude more tokens.
quote: agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats.

claim: Multi-agent systems excel at valuable breadth-first tasks with heavy parallelization, information exceeding one context window, and many complex tools, and are a poor fit when agents share context or have many dependencies.
why: Its internal eval had a multi-agent Opus 4 lead with Sonnet 4 subagents beating single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2% on breadth-first research.
check: Flag shared-context or dependency-heavy work split across agents.
quote: some domains that require all agents to share the same context or involve many dependencies between agents are not a good fit for multi-agent systems today.

claim: Coding tasks have fewer parallelizable parts than research, and agents are not yet great at real-time delegation to each other.
why: This is the post's stated reason coding fits multi-agent systems less well; it is older than the Claude Code subagent and team docs.
check: Treat parallel code-writing subagents with more suspicion than parallel research ones.
quote: most coding tasks involve fewer truly parallelizable tasks than research, and LLM agents are not yet great at coordinating and delegating to other agents in real time.

claim: A delegation brief to a worker should give an objective, an output format, guidance on tools and sources, and clear task boundaries.
why: Without detail, subagents duplicate work, leave gaps or misread the task.
check: Look at the delegation instructions in agent bodies and the lead's prompts for these four elements.
quote: Each subagent needs an objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries.

claim: Short vague delegation instructions caused subagents to misinterpret the task or repeat each other's searches.
why: In the example one subagent explored a 2021 crisis while two others duplicated work on 2025.
check: Flag one-line delegation prompts such as 'research X' with no division of labor.
quote: Without detailed task descriptions, agents duplicate work, leave gaps, or fail to find necessary information.

claim: Embed effort-scaling rules in lead prompts: about 1 agent and 3-10 tool calls for simple lookups, 2-4 subagents for comparisons, and more than 10 for complex research.
why: Agents struggle to judge effort and early versions overinvested in simple queries, even spawning 50 subagents.
check: Check whether orchestrator prompts say how many workers a task of a given size merits.
quote: Simple fact-finding requires just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls, direct comparisons might need 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each, and complex research might use more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities.

claim: Each tool or specialist needs a distinct purpose and a clear description, because bad descriptions send agents down wrong paths.
why: With many MCP tools, agents meet unseen tools of widely varying description quality.
check: Look for subagents and MCP tools with overlapping or vague descriptions.
quote: Bad tool descriptions can send agents down completely wrong paths, so each tool needs a distinct purpose and a clear description.

claim: Having subagents write work to external storage and return lightweight references to the coordinator avoids information loss and token overhead.
why: Routing large outputs through the lead causes a game of telephone.
check: For large structured outputs, check that workers write files and return paths rather than the full content.
quote: Subagents call tools to store their work in external systems, then pass lightweight references back to the coordinator.

claim: The research system's lead ran subagents synchronously, so the lead could not steer them and subagents could not coordinate; this is older than Claude Code, where subagents default to background and named subagents can message each other.
why: The post expected asynchronous execution to pay off as models improve.
check: Do not apply the post's synchronous-execution limitation to current Claude Code subagents.
quote: Currently, our lead agents execute subagents synchronously, waiting for each set of subagents to complete before proceeding.

claim: The lead should start 3-5 subagents in parallel and each subagent should use 3 or more tools in parallel, which cut research time by up to 90 percent.
why: Sequential searches were painfully slow; note this is a smaller fan-out than Claude Code's 20-subagent limit or workflow scale.
check: Flag serial chains of independent subagents.
quote: the lead agent spins up 3-5 subagents in parallel rather than serially

claim: Prompt multi-agent systems as frameworks for collaboration defining division of labor and effort budgets, since small changes to the lead can unpredictably change subagent behavior.
why: Multi-agent systems have emergent behaviors.
check: Re-test the whole delegation chain after editing the orchestrator or a worker prompt.
quote: Multi-agent systems have emergent behaviors, which arise without specific programming.

claim: For long work across context windows, use an initializer session that writes the environment, a feature list and a progress file, then have each later session do one feature and leave a clean state.
why: Without it agents tried to one-shot the project or declared it done early.
check: For long-running agent setups, look for a progress artifact and a feature list the next session reads first.
quote: the next iteration of the coding agent was then asked to work on only one feature at a time.

claim: Store a long-run feature checklist as JSON, since the model is less likely to inappropriately change JSON than Markdown.
why: Coding agents were told to edit only the passes field.
check: Check that status trackers agents must not rewrite are structured data.
quote: the model is less likely to inappropriately change or overwrite JSON files compared to Markdown files.

claim: Agents must be explicitly prompted to verify features end-to-end, for example with browser automation, because by default they mark features complete without proper testing.
why: Unit tests and curl did not reveal that the feature failed end-to-end.
check: Check that implementer prompts or a verifier role require end-to-end verification before marking done.
quote: tendency to mark a feature as complete without proper testing

claim: Anthropic called it an open question whether one general coding agent or specialized agents (testing, QA, cleanup) perform better.
why: So no source proves that splitting roles beats one well-prompted agent; the initializer and coding agents there differed only in initial prompt.
check: Treat a large role roster as a hypothesis to justify, not a best practice.
quote: it’s still unclear whether a single, general-purpose coding agent performs best across contexts, or if better performance can be achieved through a multi-agent architecture

claim: To use a cheaper model for a sub-task without invalidating the prompt cache, spawn a subagent on that model and keep the main loop on one model.
why: Switching models mid-session invalidates the cache.
check: Flag setups that switch the main session's model mid-task for cost.
quote: Spawn a **subagent** with the cheaper model for the sub-task; keep the main loop on one model.
